note.note:
HISTORY AND PHYSICAL (H&P)

History:
- 32-year-old male plastic-surgery doctor presents with recurrent, episodic neurologic symptoms for ~6–8 weeks.
  • Initial frequency once per week/month → now several episodes per day.  
  • Each episode lasts “a few days,” then complete return to baseline.
- Episode features (right-sided):
  • Pins-and-needles and numbness in right hand.  
  • Subjective weakness of right arm and right leg; colleague notices abnormal gait.  
  • Difficulty holding a coffee cup; transient sensation of “something” in throat during episodes.  
  • Occasional fatigue and nausea.
- No speech difficulty, no visual loss, no persistent dysphagia, no headaches reported.
- No current symptoms at time of consultation.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: none reported.
- Surgical history: none mentioned.
- Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not stated).
- Medications: Aspirin 75 mg daily (self-initiated; dose/route/frequency not documented beyond daily use).
- Family history: Father underwent carotid endarterectomy for stroke prevention.
- Social: Non-smoker; lives with wife; employed as a doctor (plastic surgery).

Physical Examination:
- Modality: Video call (video lost part-way).  
- General: Alert, oriented, conversant; no acute distress.  
- Neurologic: Speech clear; no focal deficit apparent during call.  
- Gait, cranial nerves, motor/sensory testing: Not recorded (remote consult).  
- Cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal: Not recorded.  
- Vitals: Not recorded.

Impression:
Recurrent transient unilateral neurologic episodes concerning for transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) versus other demyelinating/neurologic pathology.  
Top DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Recurrent TIA – unilateral sensory-motor events, strong family history.  
2. Relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis – age and duration compatible, though strictly right-sided symptoms argue against (consider if vascular work-up negative).

Management Plan:
- Urgent referral to hospital TIA/​stroke clinic (target appointment within 1–2 days).  
  • Planned carotid ultrasound and brain imaging per clinic protocol.  
  • Contact numbers (PALS and TIA clinic) provided to patient to confirm scheduling.
- Safety-netting: If symptoms recur and persist or worsen, attend Emergency Department immediately.  
- Re-contact GP service for any interim concerns.
- No medication changes documented; aspirin use acknowledged but not specifically addressed.

Patient Summary:
32-year-old man with 6-week history of intermittent right-sided paresthesia and weakness now increasing in frequency. Presentation raises concern for TIAs; urgent specialist evaluation arranged.

Key Takeaways:
- Attend TIA clinic within the next 48 hours; call clinic today/tomorrow to confirm slot.  
- Go to A&E immediately if an episode occurs and does not quickly resolve.  
- Keep GP informed of any delays or new symptoms.

Next Steps:
- Await TIA clinic assessment including carotid Doppler and neuro-imaging.  
- Further management guided by clinic findings (e.g., antiplatelet optimization, additional neurology referral if non-vascular etiology suspected).

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing elements: vitals, full systems review, detailed neurologic exam, reaction details to penicillin, confirmation of alcohol intake, clarification of aspirin plan.  
● Transcript/DDx conflicts: None noted (both align on vascular vs demyelinating considerations).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional audio/video loss limited physical assessment.
